item.title: China’s Economic Growth Accelerates to 4.5% in Third Quarter
item.description: China’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, official data showed on Monday, easing pressure on policymakers to step up stimulus even as weak consumer spending and a deepening property downturn clouded the outlook. Gross domestic product expanded 4.5% from a year earlier, …
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded:
China’s economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, official data showed on Monday, easing pressure on policymakers to step up stimulus even as weak consumer spending and a deepening property downturn clouded the outlook.

Gross domestic product expanded 4.5% from a year earlier, the National Bureau of Statistics said, beating a Reuters poll forecast of 4.4% and accelerating from 4.3% in the second quarter, the weakest pace in more than three years.

On a quarterly basis, the economy grew 1.2%, above expectations for a 1.1% increase and up from 0.9% in the previous three months.

The figures put Beijing’s full-year growth target of 4.5% to 5% within reach, but highlighted an uneven recovery as manufacturing and exports continued to outpace domestic demand.

“Growth has stabilised, but it has not yet entered a self-sustaining recovery,” said Raymond Yeung, chief China economist at ANZ in Hong Kong.

ANZ maintained its 2026 growth forecast at 4.6%, although Yeung said risks remained tilted to the downside because of weak domestic demand, persistent deflationary pressure and the ongoing property slump.

September activity data showed modest improvements in industrial production and consumption.

Industrial output rose 5.5% from a year earlier, matching expectations and accelerating from 5.2% in August. Retail sales increased 1.1%, beating forecasts for a 0.6% gain and improving from August’s 0.4% rise.

But the pickup in spending remained subdued. Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said retail sales barely grew from a year earlier after adjusting for inflation.

Growth over the first nine months reached 4.6%, Zhang said, potentially reducing the need for a significant shift in policy before the end of the year.

Investment figures underscored the economy’s underlying strains. Fixed asset investment fell 7.2% in January-September from a year earlier, slightly better than the forecast decline of 7.3% but unchanged from the pace recorded in the first eight months.

Property investment dropped 20.6%, steepening from a 19.9% decline in January-August as the sector continued to struggle to stabilise.

China’s resilience this year has rested heavily on robust manufacturing and booming exports linked to artificial intelligence investment, while cautious households and weaker private investment have held back domestic activity.

“External demand is still keeping the economy afloat,” said Ho Woei Chen, an economist at UOB in Singapore, who forecasts full-year growth of 4.5%.

Targeted support was likely to continue, she said, but broad-based easing appeared unlikely while growth remained on track to reach the bottom of the government’s target range.

That reliance on overseas demand leaves China exposed to a cooling global AI investment cycle, which could weaken demand for technology products and components. A deal with the European Union to curb Chinese hybrid-vehicle shipments could also weigh on a fast-growing export industry.

Andy Ji, an analyst at ITC Markets in Shanghai, said the stronger GDP and retail sales figures reduced the urgency for immediate broad-based easing, although the economy remained heavily dependent on exports and state support.

“The active policy debate is fiscal,” he said.

A Reuters poll forecasts China’s growth will slow to 4.5% this year from 5.0% in 2025, before easing further to 4.4% in 2027.
